overview: The Navajo, or Diné, are a living Indigenous people whose homeland spans the American Southwest. Navajo Nation sources call it Diné Bikéyah. This shared card covers the map’s Navajo, Navaho and Diné Bikéyah labels. Their different outlines and 1492 to 1650 date windows are imported coverage, not reliable borders or the beginning and ending of a single state.

periods.title: Homeland communities and colonial pressures
periods.summary: Navajo communities developed varied homes, crafts and ways of making a living; later pueblitos record both domestic life and insecurity.

periods.title: Forced removal and imprisonment
periods.summary: United States forces removed Navajo people to Bosque Redondo, followed by years of confinement.

periods.title: Return and a continuing nation
periods.summary: The treaty enabled return, followed by rebuilding and later changes in national government.

items.text: In northwestern New Mexico, Navajo builders made small masonry pueblitos during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Many stood on boulders or outcrops with wide views. They provided shelter and cooking space as well as refuge during conflict, so a defensible position also had to work as a home.

Pueblito remains include roofs, hooded fireplaces, nearby hogan foundations and small openings used to check a doorway. A family could cook, keep out weather and watch an entrance in the same compact building. These practical architectural details survive alongside the story of warfare.

Diné weavers adopted wool from introduced churra sheep and incorporated it into their textile traditions. The upright loom let makers build a cloth through the patient crossing of threads. Behind a finished blanket stood an entire chain of work, beginning with keeping the animals alive.

At Hubbell Trading Post, established in Ganado in 1878, Navajo customers exchanged blankets, wool, sheep and pelts for goods such as flour, coffee, tools and cloth. The post also supplied news and jobs. A shopping trip could therefore carry both household supplies and neighborhood information home.

The predominantly red geometric style called Ganado Red became associated with the trading post. Hubbell promoted particular designs for outside buyers, while Navajo weavers supplied the artistry and labor. Rugs linked skilled household production to a market whose tastes could influence what makers were asked to weave.

A 2016 Hubbell workshop offered hands-on dyeing, spinning and weaving, together with learning about Churro sheep. The program had begun in 2000 to share fiber skills and animal husbandry. Before anyone could weave a beautiful design, the wool still had to become usable yarn.

In 1864, United States forces drove Navajo people from their homeland to Bosque Redondo in eastern New Mexico. In a 2018 anniversary message, Navajo leadership remembered four years of imprisonment and suffering there. The Long Walk was forced displacement, not a voluntary migration to find better farmland.

The treaty concluded at Fort Sumner on June 1, 1868 allowed a return home. Its text also promised the purchase of 15,000 sheep and goats and support for the journey. Reading the document makes rebuilding tangible: families needed animals, food and transport as well as permission to leave.

The first modern Navajo council was created in 1923, and reforms in 1989 reorganized national government through separated branches. These are changes in the institutions of a continuing people. They should not be mistaken for the invention of Navajo community life or its first traditions of leadership.

The first group of 29 Navajo Marine recruits arrived for training in May 1942. They helped develop a military code with an initial vocabulary of 211 terms and a system for spelling English letters. The achievement combined language expertise, memorization and radio training; it was more than ordinary conversation overheard on a battlefield.

sections.title: Family introductions, learning and a living language

items.text: Navajo scholar Shelly C. Lowe explains that her clan comes through her mother and passes to her children. Introducing clan relationships and home community helps people place one another within a network of relatives. An introduction can be a miniature family map rather than just a name.

Remembering school in Ganado, Lowe describes designing rugs on craft paper, beadwork and other cultural arts in class. She also heard Navajo from school cooks and aides as well as relatives. Language and skills traveled through ordinary encounters, from the classroom to the people preparing lunch.

Written language sample: yá’át’ééh, translated by Lowe as “It is good,” is a Navajo greeting printed in her 2022 interview. This is an attested modern spelling of a living language. It is not presented as an inscription surviving from the map’s sixteenth-century window.

ending.text: The Diné endured forced removal and returned after the 1868 treaty. Their nation, families and language continue, with government institutions changing over time. None of the imported map endpoints should be read as the extinction of the Navajo people.
